title: Perioperative Care: Verify Before, Breathe and Move After
bottomLine: Before surgery, verify identity, procedure/site, consent status, allergies, NPO status, medications, baseline data and required preparation; the provider obtains informed consent, while nursing verifies that consent is present and alerts the team if questions remain. After surgery, airway/breathing, circulation, pain/sedation, bleeding, urine, nausea and early mobility/respiratory prevention dominate.
recognize: Pre-op discrepancies in identity, site, consent, anticoagulants or NPO status are stop-and-clarify problems
Post-op respiratory depression, hemorrhage, urinary retention, DVT/PE, delirium and infection are major complications
Older adults are especially vulnerable to delirium and deconditioning
assess: Pre-op medication/allergy/NPO and baseline vitals
Post-op airway, respiratory rate/quality, SpO2, BP/HR/perfusion, sedation/pain, dressing/drains, urine and neuro status
Mobility/fall risk and nausea
actions: Use pre-procedure verification and time-out systems
Post-op support airway, cough/deep breathe/incentive spirometry as ordered, mobilize early and use VTE prevention
Treat pain/nausea while monitoring sedation
Escalate bleeding, respiratory compromise or acute neuro change
diagnostics: Post-op testing is symptom/procedure driven; routine tests should not distract from bedside deterioration
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants, diabetes drugs and other medications have procedure-specific hold/resume plans
Opioids and sedatives require respiratory/sedation monitoring
teaching: Pre-op medication/NPO instructions, postoperative breathing/mobility/pain plan and wound warning signs
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN perioperative roles vary by state and facility. The nurse does not obtain the surgeon's informed consent but must identify missing/unclear consent before the procedure proceeds.
examTrap: Explaining surgical risks and asking the patient to sign consent after sedating premedication has already been given.
oneLinePearl: Before surgery verify; after surgery breathe, perfuse, bleed-check, move.

title: Pain Management: Treat the Person, Reassess the Effect
bottomLine: Pain is assessed through the patient's report plus function and physiologic context. Use an age/cognition-appropriate scale, treat with multimodal strategies when possible, and reassess both benefit and adverse effects. Sedation and respiratory depression can make an opioid unsafe even when pain remains high.
recognize: Pain behavior varies by culture, age, cognition and prior opioid exposure
Chronic pain goals often focus on function rather than zero pain
New severe pain out of proportion can signal ischemia, compartment syndrome or other emergency
assess: Location, quality, intensity, timing, aggravating/relieving factors and functional impact
Sedation/respiration with opioids
Neuropathic versus nociceptive features and psychosocial contributors without dismissing pain
actions: Use ordered pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic strategies
Time medication around activity when helpful
Reassess at an appropriate interval and document response
Escalate new unexplained severe pain or treatment toxicity
diagnostics: Pain score is not a diagnostic test; new pain may require cause-specific evaluation
medicationSafety: Acetaminophen total daily dose includes combination products
NSAIDs carry renal/GI/cardiovascular risks
Opioids require sedation/respiratory monitoring
redFlags: Pain plus shock or rigid abdomen
teaching: Use the agreed pain/function goal, medication timing and non-drug strategies; report dangerous sedation or new pain pattern
scopeAndDelegation: Assistive personnel can report pain scores but the nurse assesses the pain pattern, medication safety and response.
examTrap: Giving additional opioid solely because the numeric pain score is high while the patient is difficult to arouse.
oneLinePearl: Pain treatment is assessment plus function plus safe reassessment.
sourceBasis: CDC 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain

title: Dysphagia and Aspiration: Swallow Safety Before the Tray
bottomLine: Coughing, wet voice, pocketing, drooling, recurrent pneumonia or neurologic injury can signal dysphagia. Keep high-risk patients NPO until the authorized swallow screen/evaluation is completed, position upright for feeding, use the prescribed texture/liquid strategy and stop feeding if aspiration signs occur.
recognize: Coughing/choking with meals, wet/gurgly voice, prolonged chewing, pocketing
Silent aspiration can occur without cough
Stroke, Parkinson disease, dementia and neuromuscular disease increase risk
assess: Alertness, oral motor control, cough/voice and ability to manage secretions
Respiratory status before/during/after meals
Prescribed diet texture and feeding assistance needs
actions: Keep NPO when swallow safety is not established after acute neuro event
Use upright positioning and slow small bites/sips according to SLP plan
Check mouth for pocketed food
Stop feeding and escalate choking/aspiration symptoms
diagnostics: Bedside swallow screening identifies risk; instrumental studies such as videofluoroscopy or FEES define physiology when needed
medicationSafety: Do not crush medications into food unless the formulation and swallow plan permit
Sedatives can worsen swallow safety
teaching: Follow exact texture, positioning and pacing instructions; do not 'test' thin liquids at home if they are restricted
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN follows swallow precautions and reports aspiration signs; diet texture and swallow therapy are SLP/provider-directed.
examTrap: Giving water to a new stroke patient to see whether they can swallow before a required screen.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association stroke dysphagia principles

title: Nasogastric Tubes: Verify Before Use, Protect From Aspiration
bottomLine: Before the first use of a newly placed NG tube, placement must be confirmed using the approved method; auscultating injected air is unreliable. For decompression, maintain ordered suction and patency; for feeding/medications, use placement checks, head elevation and flushing per policy.
recognize: Tube migration can cause aspiration
Decompression failure can worsen distention/vomiting
High continuous suction can injure mucosa or disturb electrolytes depending on device/order
assess: External tube length/marking and approved placement verification
Abdominal distention, nausea/vomiting and output
Respiratory status and oral/nasal skin
actions: Confirm initial placement before first use
Keep suction setting exactly as ordered
Provide oral/nasal care and flush per protocol
Stop use and reassess if tube displacement is suspected
diagnostics: Radiographic confirmation is commonly used for initial feeding-tube placement depending on type/location and facility policy
medicationSafety: Do not crush enteric-coated or extended-release drugs
Give medications separately with appropriate flushes
teaching: Explain tube purpose and the need to avoid pulling/manipulating it
scopeAndDelegation: NG insertion and use depend on competency/policy. PN/LVN must not use an unverified tube merely because aspiration of gastric-appearing contents was obtained.
examTrap: Confirming NG placement by injecting air and listening over the stomach.
oneLinePearl: Tube placement needs evidence, not a whoosh.

title: Parenteral Nutrition: Glucose, Line Infection, Electrolytes
bottomLine: Parenteral nutrition is concentrated nutrition delivered through vascular access and carries major hyperglycemia, electrolyte, refeeding, infection and line risks. Use dedicated aseptic access according to policy, monitor glucose/electrolytes and do not abruptly stop a high-dextrose infusion without a safe plan because hypoglycemia can occur.
recognize: Central PN usually requires central venous access due to osmolarity
Refeeding shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium
Catheter bloodstream infection can present with fever/rigors without dramatic site redness
assess: Glucose, electrolytes, weight/fluid status and nutrition response
Line site/dressing and fever
Liver tests/triglycerides and other labs as ordered
actions: Use infusion pump and prescribed rate
Maintain strict aseptic line access and dedicated lumen when required
If PN is unexpectedly interrupted, follow protocol for dextrose/monitoring rather than simply leaving the patient without carbohydrate
Escalate infection or severe metabolic changes
diagnostics: Lab frequency depends on stability and refeeding risk
medicationSafety: Do not add medications to PN without pharmacy authorization
Insulin may be part of the plan but requires glucose monitoring
teaching: Home PN users need meticulous line care and infection/glucose warning signs
scopeAndDelegation: PN management and central-line access depend on state/facility competency. Formula changes are pharmacy/nutrition/prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Abruptly stopping a high-dextrose PN infusion and doing nothing because the next bag is delayed.
oneLinePearl: PN: pump, glucose, electrolytes, sterile line.

title: Peripheral IV Complications: Infiltration Is Not Phlebitis
bottomLine: Infiltration is nonvesicant fluid leaking into tissue; extravasation involves a vesicant; phlebitis is vein inflammation. Stop the infusion when a complication is suspected, assess the site and drug, remove or preserve the catheter according to the specific protocol, elevate/antidote/compress as indicated and restart elsewhere when safe.
recognize: Infiltration: cool/pale swelling, slowed infusion, discomfort
Phlebitis: redness, warmth, tenderness, cord-like vein
Extravasation can cause blistering/necrosis and needs drug-specific management
assess: Site color, temperature, swelling, pain and neurovascular status
Infusing medication/fluid and vesicant properties
Catheter function and amount potentially infiltrated
actions: Stop infusion
For simple infiltration/phlebitis, remove catheter when appropriate and treat site per protocol
For vesicant extravasation, do not flush and preserve access if aspiration/antidote is required
Document and reassess tissue
diagnostics: Diagnosis is clinical; severe tissue injury may need specialist evaluation
medicationSafety: Warm/cold compress selection is agent-specific for extravasation
Never flush suspected vesicant into tissue
teaching: Report burning, swelling, leaking or tightness at IV site immediately
scopeAndDelegation: Peripheral IV insertion/medication scope varies. PN/LVN must follow the exact extravasation policy for the infusing agent.
examTrap: Flushing a painful swollen IV to 'make sure it is still patent.'
oneLinePearl: Swollen IV? Stop first, identify what leaked, then use the correct protocol.
sourceBasis: Infusion Nurses Society Infusion Therapy Standards of Practice

title: Constipation and Fecal Impaction: Find the Cause Before Adding Laxatives
bottomLine: Constipation management starts with cause, duration, medications, hydration, mobility and obstruction red flags. Fecal impaction can cause rectal pressure, abdominal distention, urinary retention or overflow liquid stool; do not treat suspected obstruction or acute surgical abdomen with routine stimulant laxatives.
recognize: Opioids, anticholinergics, immobility, dehydration and neurologic disease are common causes
Overflow diarrhea can occur around an impaction
New severe constipation with vomiting/distention may be obstruction
assess: Usual bowel pattern, stool, pain/distention, nausea/vomiting and flatus
Medication and fluid/fiber/activity history
Rectal examination only when clinically indicated and within policy; avoid in selected neutropenic/thrombocytopenic patients
actions: Use hydration, mobility, fiber and bowel regimen according to cause
Use prophylactic stimulant/osmotic regimen with chronic opioids when ordered
Treat impaction with suppository/enema/manual intervention only according to assessment/order
Escalate obstruction or peritonitis
diagnostics: Imaging/labs are selected when obstruction, severe illness or secondary causes are suspected
medicationSafety: Magnesium laxatives can accumulate in kidney failure
Frequent stimulant or phosphate enemas can cause electrolyte problems
Bulk fiber can worsen obstruction if fluid/intestinal passage is inadequate
redFlags: Autonomic dysreflexia risk during rectal manipulation
teaching: Regular activity, fluids/fiber when appropriate and medication-specific bowel plans
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN assesses bowel pattern and performs ordered bowel interventions within policy; do not delegate assessment of suspected impaction/obstruction to assistive personnel.
examTrap: Interpreting watery stool as proof that there is no fecal impaction.
oneLinePearl: Constipation plus overflow can still be impaction.

title: Mobility and Transfers: Assess First, Device Second
bottomLine: Safe mobility begins with current strength, weight-bearing status, cognition, orthostasis, pain and lines/tubes. Use the correct number of staff and lift/transfer device; do not manually lift a dependent patient when safe patient-handling equipment is indicated.
recognize: Fall risk changes after sedation, illness, surgery or medication changes
Orthostatic symptoms can appear at first mobilization
Dragging a patient across sheets causes shear and staff injury
assess: Ability to sit, stand, bear weight and follow commands
BP/symptoms with position changes when indicated
Lines/drains and prescribed mobility restrictions
actions: Use gait belt/lift/slide equipment according to patient ability and policy
Dangle and progress activity as clinically appropriate
Use nonskid footwear and clear path
Stop and reassess dizziness, weakness, chest pain or dyspnea
medicationSafety: Sedatives, antihypertensives and opioids can increase fall/orthostatic risk
teaching: Use call bell and prescribed device; rise slowly and do not transfer alone when assistance is ordered
scopeAndDelegation: Assistive personnel can ambulate stable patients within a defined plan. The nurse evaluates new or changed mobility and determines when the plan must be revised/escalated.
examTrap: Having one staff member pivot-transfer a fully dependent patient because it seems faster than obtaining the lift.
oneLinePearl: Transfer safety: assess ability, respect restrictions, use the right equipment.
sourceBasis: OSHA/ANA Safe Patient Handling and Mobility Principles

title: Fluid Volume: Is the Patient Dry, Wet, or Both?
bottomLine: Fluid assessment combines history, weight, intake/output, blood pressure/perfusion, mucous membranes, edema/JVP, lung sounds, urine and labs. A patient can have edema and still be intravascularly depleted, so avoid deciding fluid therapy from swelling or one lab alone.
recognize: Volume depletion: orthostasis, tachycardia, poor perfusion, dry mucosa, low urine
Volume excess: weight gain, edema, JVD, crackles, hypertension, dyspnea
Cirrhosis/nephrotic states can have third-spacing with low effective circulating volume
assess: Daily weight trend using consistent conditions
Strict intake/output when indicated
BP/perfusion, edema/JVP, lungs and urine
Sodium, creatinine, hematocrit and other labs in context
actions: Give or restrict fluid according to the diagnosed problem/order
Reassess after bolus or diuresis
Escalate pulmonary edema, shock or severe sodium change
diagnostics: No single sign is perfectly sensitive; integrate trends and clinical context
medicationSafety: IV fluids can cause overload
Diuretics can cause intravascular depletion
Fluid orders need modification in heart/kidney/liver disease based on response
teaching: Daily weight and individualized sodium/fluid instructions when used at home
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN can collect/trend fluid data and administer ordered fluids/diuretics; independent resuscitation or fluid-restriction changes require protocol/provider authority.
examTrap: Giving a large fluid bolus solely because a patient has low urine output despite crackles, JVD and rapid weight gain.
oneLinePearl: Fluid status is a pattern, not a single sign.

title: Hospital Sleep and Delirium Prevention: Protect the Day-Night Cycle
bottomLine: Sleep disruption, immobility, sensory deprivation, pain, urinary retention, constipation and sedating/anticholinergic drugs contribute to hospital delirium. Support daytime mobility/light, nighttime quiet, orientation, glasses/hearing aids and clustered care while investigating any acute confusion for a medical cause.
recognize: Hypoactive delirium may look sleepy or withdrawn rather than agitated
Sleep medications can worsen falls and confusion
New confusion is not normal aging
assess: Baseline cognition, attention/fluctuation and sleep pattern
Pain, oxygenation, glucose, medications, urine/bowel, infection and sensory aids
Daytime activity and nighttime interruptions
actions: Promote daytime mobilization and orientation
Reduce avoidable nighttime noise/light/procedures
Ensure glasses/hearing aids are available
Avoid routine restraints and sedatives when safer alternatives work
diagnostics: Use validated delirium screening; investigate the underlying cause rather than ordering sedatives first
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines and anticholinergics commonly worsen delirium outside selected withdrawal indications
Melatonin/sleep agents do not replace nonpharmacologic prevention
teaching: Family can help with orientation and familiar routines; bring sensory aids when possible
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN coordinates bedside delirium-prevention measures and identifies acute change; assistive staff can support mobility/orientation within the plan.
examTrap: Requesting a sedative first for a newly confused older adult without assessing reversible causes.
oneLinePearl: Protect sleep, movement and senses—but treat delirium as a medical change.
sourceBasis: American Geriatrics Society delirium prevention principles
